newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Canadian wheat board sees bullish long term demand.
newsitem.headline: Canadian wheat board sees bullish long term demand.

text.p: World wheat prices are expected to firm in real terms over the next 10 years as strong demand puts pressure on supplies, Brian Oleson, Executive Director for Planning at the Canadian Wheat Board, said on Wednesday.
Oleson noted that world population was growing annually by 1.6 percent, or by 90 million people, and incomes were soaring in many key countries, notably in Southeast Asia.
"The overall picture for the grain industry is fairly bright," he told an Agra Europe grain conference.
Constraints on the use of export subsidies, monitored by the World Trade Organisation, should also be positive for grain prices, he added.
But he warned that the supply/demand balance is likely to be much more precarious and that price instability will increase considerably.
World wheat trade is seen rising to 118 million tonnes in 2005, from just under 100 million tonnes between 1989-93, with most of the increase in the Asia Pacific region.
Chinese wheat imports are expected to rise by almost 35 percent to 16 million tonnes by 2005 making it by far the world's largest importer.
The increase is expected despite a drop in wheat imports this year of at least four million tonnes to less than eight million tonnes after a bumper crop.

Over the next decade, Canada's share of world wheat exports is seen rising to 21 percent, from 19 percent. It is forecast retaining its position as the world's largest supplier of durum wheat, with exports rising by 50 percent to 3.4 million tonnes.

Oleson said that the projections, based on a study completed in 1995, would need to be revised if yields grew by more than the forecast rate of slightly more than one percent. Other factors, such as abnormal weather could also upset the scenario.
